records.name_note: Admissible sources split on the primary common name. NC State's dedicated Eruca vesicaria page lists its Common Name(s) alphabetically (Arugula, Eruca, Garden Rocket, Gharghir, Mediterranean Salad, Rocket, Rocket Salad, Roquette, Ruchtetta, Rucola, Rucoli, Rugula, Rugulas, Salad Rocket), in the same order as its page-title parenthetical, so the list leads with Arugula; its Description also opens with Arugula, and Arugula is used for common_name on that basis. RHS's dedicated Eruca vesicaria page (Name Status: Correct) instead gives "rocket 4" as the common-name subtitle under its H1 and lists arugula as its only other common name. RHS's Eruca vesicaria subsp. sativa page (also served at the URL for the synonym Eruca sativa) gives "garden rocket" as its subtitle and lists arugula first in its Other common names line.
records.toxicity_detail: No admissible source addresses toxicity to cats or dogs for this species: NC State's dedicated Eruca vesicaria page has no Poison section and no Problem-for-Cats/Problem-for-Dogs tags, and the RHS, MoBot, Clemson and PSU pages are also silent, so nothing is established about pet safety. NC State's Edibility field reads: "Leaves, flowers, seed pods, and seeds are edible. Harvest leaves and seed pods when young as they get tough and bitter with age. Harvest only as needed as leaves do not keep long in the refrigerator after harvesting." RHS's dedicated Eruca vesicaria page says more broadly: "All of the plant is edible with a peppery taste". These are human-edibility statements, not pet-toxicity findings.
unknowns: toxic_to_pets left null: NC State's dedicated Eruca vesicaria page has no Poison section and no Problem-for-Cats/Problem-for-Dogs tags; no other admissible source (Clemson, UF/IFAS, PSU, RHS) addresses cat or dog toxicity for arugula, so there is no basis to set true or false.

chill_damage_f left null: no admissible source states a damage-onset temperature, and sources disagree qualitatively on frost. Clemson's arugula paragraph says 'Harvest arugula before freezing temperatures arrive since it is not tolerant of frost.' NC State's dedicated page says 'It also tolerates wet, mucky soil to some degree as well as light frosts.' UMD's multi-crop Fall Vegetable Gardening page lists arugula among 'Hardy crops (will withstand a hard frost)'. NC State's hardiness zones (2a-11b), MoBot's Zone 2 to 11 and RHS's hardiness ratings (H6 on the Eruca vesicaria page, H4 on the subsp. sativa page) are survival ratings, not damage onsets.

day_f_min/max and night_f_min/max left null: no admissible source gives numeric degree-F growing-temperature ranges for arugula specifically; sources only describe qualitative effects (warm temperatures cause bolting, freezing temperatures should be avoided at harvest) without figures.

humidity_need/humidity_pct_min/humidity_pct_max left null: no admissible source states a humidity requirement or percentage range for arugula (PSU's disease-management page notes bacterial pathogens thrive in humid conditions, but that is a disease-risk note, not a plant humidity need).

light_fc_min/light_fc_good/direct_sun_hours_max left null: NC State's '6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day' text is the site-wide definition text attached to its Full Sun category legend, not species-specific prose about arugula, so per the rules it cannot supply direct_sun_hours_max; no other admissible source gives foot-candle or hour figures for arugula.

soil_ph_max left null: NC State's Soil pH field is the closed band 'Neutral (6.0-8.0)', but RHS's dedicated Eruca vesicaria page lists pH as 'Acid or Neutral or Alkaline' (its subsp. sativa page: 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral'), so alkaline soils are acceptable and no ceiling is taken from the band's top. Clemson's 'Maintain a soil pH of 6.0 to 6.5' is group guidance for the greens collectively, not an arugula-specific range.

water_regime and the water_* fields left null: no admissible source gives an arugula watering cadence. Clemson's arugula paragraph says only 'Thin plants to 9 inches apart and provide adequate moisture.', and its 'Water deeply when necessary to encourage sufficient root growth.' is group guidance for all the greens. MoBot's dedicated subsp. sativa page has a structured Water field of 'Medium to wet' and says 'It thrives in rich moist soils in full sun to part shade.' NC State tags the soil Moist and says it 'tolerates wet, mucky soil to some degree'. RHS's subsp. sativa page says 'Fairly drought resistant.' These moisture descriptors and a drought-tolerance trait pull in different directions and are not a watering instruction, so no regime is set. NC State gives container guidance (minimum 3-gallon pot) but no dry-down cadence.

fertilize_interval_days, fertilize_active_months, fertilize_strength left null: no admissible source gives a numeric fertilizing interval, active-month schedule, or dilution/strength fraction for arugula.

is_houseplant landed false: no admissible source characterizes arugula as a houseplant. NC State's Landscape Location field lists 'Container' and its separate Landscape Theme field lists 'Edible Garden', which describes outdoor container vegetable growing, not indoor houseplant use, and its USDA Plant Hardiness Zone field runs 2a-11b. The value is landed false as an outdoor garden annual rather than left null.
cool_rest_note left null: no admissible source frames a cool-temperature dormancy/rest period for arugula.

attracts_pollinators left null: searched 'Attracts', 'Pollinator', 'butterfl', 'bee', 'hummingbird', and 'Wildlife' on the NC State anchor page and all three RHS pages; none carries a structured attracts/wildlife field or an unconditional pollinator statement for this species (the two 'bee' hits on NC State/RHS were false positives -- 'Beta vulgaris' and 'flea beetles', not pollinator language).

Before setting is_edible, searched 'Poison', 'Toxic', and 'Problem for' on the NC State anchor page and on all three RHS pages; none of the four pages names a poisonous part, severity, toxic principle, preparation requirement, or pets warning for this species, so is_edible is set true with no toxicity caveat needed.

mature_height_in and mature_spread_in are taken from the NC State Plant Toolbox page because it is a species-level page for Eruca vesicaria itself (not a genus page), which the task instructions treat as the anchor over RHS. Eruca vesicaria is an annual herb, not a vine/liana/climber, so the climber exclusion (rule 4) does not apply.

All four cited pages fetched successfully via qc.py (fetch status 'ok'); none refused this machine, so no page-refusal line is needed. For reference only (not used as the recorded value): RHS independently gives Max Height 0.5-1 metres (about 19.7-39.4 in) on all three RHS pages, and Max Spread of 0-0.1 metres (0-3.9 in) on the two Eruca sativa/subsp. sativa pages versus 0.1-0.5 metres (3.9-19.7 in) on the plain 'Eruca vesicaria' RHS page -- broadly consistent with, but not overriding, the NC State species-page figures used above.

records.name_note: NC State's Common Name(s) list for Cucurbita moschata is alphabetized (Butternut Squash, Calabasa, Calabaza, Crookneck Squash, Squash, Winter Squash) and matches the order of the page-title parenthetical. Two of its entries, "Squash" and "Winter Squash," also appear in the alphabetized Common Name(s) list on NC State's dedicated Cucurbita pepo page, so they do not distinguish moschata from pepo. "Butternut Squash" is used as common_name because it is the first-listed name on this species' dedicated page, the lead item of the page-title parenthetical, and the subject of the page's description. RHS's dedicated Cucurbita moschata profile leads with the generic "squash" and lists "butternut squash" among its other common names.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State Extension Plant Toolbox tags Cucurbita moschata "#non-toxic for cats", "#non-toxic for dogs", and the co-listed "#non-toxic for horses", with no Poison section, symptom list, or poison-part list, and its Fruit Description states "Fruits and seeds are both edible." RHS's dedicated Cucurbita moschata profile disagrees in part: its Potentially harmful entry reads "Humans/Pets: If crop is bitter, don't eat or feed to pets. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling" (the same entry appears on RHS's Cucurbita pepo and Cucurbita maxima profiles).

day_f_min/max, night_f_min/max, chill_damage_f, cool_rest_note, humidity_need, humidity_pct_min/max, light_fc_min/good left null: NC State's dedicated Cucurbita moschata page has no structured temperature, chill-damage-onset, humidity or foot-candle field. RHS's dedicated Cucurbita moschata profile was located but supplies none of them either: its hardiness rating is the bare 'H2', whose site-wide legend ('tolerant of low temperatures, but not surviving being frozen (1 to 5)') is a survival band and not a damage onset, and its Cultivation line 'maintain a constant temperature of 18-21C' is a seed-germination temperature, not a day or night growing range.

direct_sun_hours_max left null per instructions: NC State's Light field states 'Full sun (6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day)', but that phrasing is the site-wide light-category legend text rather than species-specific prose, so no hour figure was recorded.

water_regime, water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm, water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est, water_estimate_basis, fertilize_interval_days, fertilize_active_months, fertilize_strength left null: neither dedicated page carries a Water Requirements or Fertility Requirements field. RHS's species-specific Cultivation paragraph does say 'Feed regularly with a high potassium fertiliser when the first fruits start to swell.', but it gives no interval, strength or months, so the fertilize fields stay null. The only water-related text is soil adjectives -- RHS's 'moisture retentive but well drained' and NC State's 'prefers moderately moist soil with full access to sunlight' -- and neither is a watering cadence.

soil_ph_max left null: NC State's Soil pH field gives a closed 'Neutral (6.0-8.0)' band, but RHS's dedicated Cucurbita moschata profile gives pH 'Acid or Neutral' (Alkaline not listed), so NC State's 8.0 ceiling is not confirmed and RHS's categories carry no numeric ceiling; RHS's inclusion of 'Acid' also differs from NC State, which does not list its Acid (<6.0) band.

outdoor_sun_exposure is limited to full_sun: NC State's structured Light field renders only 'Full sun (6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day)', and RHS's dedicated Cucurbita moschata profile has a Position field of 'Full sun', which corroborates full_sun and adds no part-sun or part-shade value.

Two admissible dedicated single-species pages were used: NC State Extension's Plant Toolbox page and RHS plant profile 139350 (title 'Cucurbita moschata | squash', Name Status 'Correct'). A supporting citation to NC State's separate Cucurbita pepo page was used solely for the name_note cross-species contrast, not as a source of Cucurbita moschata facts.

mature_height_in and mature_spread_in left null: Cucurbita moschata is a climber, not a self-supporting plant. NC State's Cucurbita moschata page gives a 'Dimensions: Height: 4 ft. 0 in. - 10 ft. 0 in. / Width: 3 ft. 0 in. - 25 ft. 0 in.' block but also lists 'Habit/Form: Climbing' and 'Climbing Method: Tendrils'; RHS's Cucurbita moschata page independently confirms 'Habit: Trailing' and describes 'trailing vines in excess of 4m (13ft) long'. Per the climber rule, these figures describe vine run/reach, not plant stature, so all four size fields are left null rather than populated from either page's Height/Width or Max Height/Max Spread figures.

attracts_pollinators left null: no page states an unconditional pollinator-attraction claim. Searched NC State Cucurbita moschata for 'Attracts' (0 hits), 'Pollinator' (3 hits — all landscape-use suggestions like 'Vegetable, Herb and Mostly Native Pollinator Garden' or photo captions, not an attracts field or statement), 'bee', 'butterfl' (only matches the cultivar name 'Butterfly'), 'moth' (0), 'hummingbird' (0); its 'Play Value' field lists 'Wildlife Food Source', which is about food (seeds/fruit), not pollination. Searched RHS Cucurbita moschata for 'Attracts' (0 hits), 'Pollinator' (0 hits), 'butterfl' (0), and found no pollinator-attractant tag or statement. No unconditional support found on either page, so left null rather than false or inferred from the edible-genus context.

RHS Cucurbita moschata page carries a pets/toxicity caveat that must be surfaced since is_edible is true: 'Potentially harmful Humans/Pets: If crop is bitter, don't eat or feed to pets. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling.' This is a conditional preparation/handling warning, not a statement that the plant is inedible, so it does not change is_edible (NC State's Fruit Description states unconditionally that fruits and seeds are both edible), but the full warning is recorded here per instructions.

https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/cucurbita-pepo/ was read as instructed but describes a different species (Cucurbita pepo, not the record's Cucurbita moschata); it contains no data usable for this record's fields and was not cited.

records.name_note: Admissible sources split on the primary common name. NC State's dedicated Prunus cerasus page (plants.ces.ncsu.edu) lists Sour Cherry as the first entry of its Common Name(s) list (Sour Cherry, Tart Cherry). RHS's dedicated species page instead shows morello cherry as the common-name subtitle beneath its Prunus cerasus heading, and lists "sour cherry" only inside its secondary "Other common names" field (alongside amarelle cherry, ceiriosen, double wild dwarf cherry, and dwarf cherry), never as its lead name. records.toxicity_detail: Cyanide is the toxic principle, in the leaves, seeds and stems (NC State Poison Part: Leaves, Seeds, Stems). NC State's Poisonous to Humans heading rates this Medium severity and gives the full symptom account: "The pits contain cyanide compounds, which are poisonous. If a couple of pits are accidentally swallowed, it will not cause poisoning. The pits are more poisonous if they are ground up/crushed or the seeds are chewed. Fruit that has not been pitted should not be blended into a smoothie. Symptoms include Gasping, weakness, excitement, pupil dilation, spasms, convulsions, coma, respiratory failure." That severity rating and symptom list are human-scoped (from the "Poisonous to Humans" block), and the same block records Causes Contact Dermatitis: No. Separately, NC State's structured Problems field tags this plant as a Problem for Cats, a Problem for Dogs and a Problem for Horses. NC State also lists the plant as Edible (Plant Type: Edible, Tree; Edibility: "Fruit is used both fresh and dried"); its Poison Part list does not include the fruit. RHS adds a handling warning under its own "Potentially harmful" field -- "Seed kernels harmful if eaten; wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling" -- and a pet note scoped only to "Pets (dogs, rabbits, rodents): Harmful if eaten," which names dogs but not cats, unlike NC State's separate cat tag.
